title: Flow Totalizer: 7 Proven Setup Steps for Accurate Totals

 Flow Totalizer: 7 Proven Setup Steps for Accurate Totals

 A flow rate tells you how fast product is moving, but the plant bill, the batch recipe and the tanker receipt all depend on how much has actually passed. A well configured totalizer turns every pulse or milliamp into a trusted running volume.

 
 K Factor Scaling 
 Pulse and 4 to 20 mA 
 Resettable Totals 
 Batch Control 
 Rollover 
 




 Every flow meter tells you a rate, yet billing, batching and stock control need the accumulated quantity. A flow totalizer integrates that rate over time, and correct K factor scaling decides whether the total can be trusted.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a flow totalizer works, how pulse and 4 to 20 mA inputs are scaled with a K factor, and how to set up resettable totals, rollover and batch control.


 
 
 
 What Is a Flow Totalizer?


 A flow totalizer is an instrument or software function that adds up the quantity of fluid passing a meter over time and shows it as a running total in litres, cubic metres, kilograms or barrels. It usually sits next to a turbine flow meter , a magnetic meter or a Coriolis meter and displays both the rate and the accumulated volume.


 
 
 Image credit: Control.com . Image courtesy of Control.com, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 Older meters used a mechanical gear register, much like a household water meter, while modern units are electronic. You will also find the same function inside smart transmitters, PLCs, DCS blocks and the flow computer used for gas and oil metering.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 How a Flow Totalizer Works


 The working principle is integration: total equals the sum of flow rate multiplied by time. With a pulse input, every pulse already represents a fixed volume, so the instrument simply counts pulses and divides by the K factor.


 
 Primary Element Rotor, magnetic field or vibrating tube senses flow

 Signal Output Pulse frequency or 4 to 20 mA current

 Input Stage Counts pulses or samples the analog value

 Scaling K factor or range converts to engineering units

 Accumulation Adds each increment to the running total

 Display and Outputs Rate, total, grand total, relays and retransmission




 With an analog input the flow totalizer first converts current into rate, then multiplies by the sampling interval and adds the result every cycle. If the transmitter sends a differential pressure signal, the totalizer must apply square root extraction before integrating, or the total will be badly wrong at low flow.


 Control.com author Shawn Dietrich describes a small rotor sensor whose datasheet gives F = 7.5 × Q, which produces 225 Hz at 30 litres per minute. He notes that a PLC with a 4 ms scan time cannot reliably catch such pulses on a normal input, so fast pulses need a hardware counter.


 Do You Know?
 A pulse input flow totalizer is naturally more accurate than an analog one, because each pulse is an exact slice of volume. An analog input adds conversion error at the transmitter, the cable and the input card before integration even starts.



 Types of Flow Totalizer Devices


 
 Mechanical Register
 Gear train on the meter drives a number wheel counter.
 Best for: water meters and PD fuel meters
 No power 

 Pulse Input Rate Totalizer
 Panel or field unit counts pulses and scales them with a K factor.
 Best for: turbine, PD and vortex meters
 Most common 

 Analog Input Totalizer
 Integrates a 4 to 20 mA rate signal over time.
 Best for: DP, magnetic and older meters
 Simple wiring 

 Built In Transmitter Totals
 Meter electronics keep several totals internally.
 Best for: modern magnetic and Coriolis meters
 No extra box 

 PLC or DCS Totalizer Block
 Software integrates the rate or counts pulses.
 Best for: plant wide reporting
 Flexible 

 Flow Computer
 Adds pressure and temperature compensation and audit logs.
 Best for: custody transfer of gas and oil
 Legal metrology 




 Positive displacement and turbine meters naturally produce pulses, so a positive displacement flow meter paired with a pulse totalizer is a classic fuel and oil combination. Magnetic and Coriolis meters offer a scaled pulse output as well as a current output, so you can choose either path.


 For a PLC based solution, the pulse wire goes to a high speed counter channel rather than a standard digital input. Slow pulses below a few hertz can still use ordinary CTU and CTD counter instructions without missing counts.


 K Factor and Scaling Formula


 The K factor is the number of pulses a meter produces for one unit of volume, for example 50 pulses per litre. It comes from the meter calibration certificate, and the method of deriving it is covered in flow meter K factor calculations .


 
 Total volume = Pulse count ÷ K factor 
 Flow rate per second = Frequency ÷ K factor 
Rate per hour = Frequency ÷ K × 3600

Example:
K = 50 pulses per litre, count = 1250000 pulses, frequency = 400 Hz
Total = 1250000 ÷ 50 = 25000 L = 25.000 m³
Rate = 400 ÷ 50 = 8 L per second
 Rate = 8 × 3600 ÷ 1000 = 28.80 m³/h 



 Yokogawa states in its YPP6300 datasheet that the field programmable K factor can be set anywhere from 0.00001 to 999,999 pulses per unit. That wide range lets one flow totalizer model serve a tiny dosing meter and a large pipeline turbine meter.

 Quick Tip
 Always copy the K factor from the latest calibration certificate, not from the catalogue nominal value. Industrial Monitor Direct notes that actual K factors can differ from nominal by 1 to 3 percent, which is a big error on a billing meter.
